idiom_name: private gate object + lock statement (System.Threading.Lock from C# 13)
implementation_notes: C# makes the lock an explicit argument, which is exactly what the guardian needs: the class keeps the state private and a dedicated gate instance beside it, and every member locks that one instance. The language reference states the guideline plainly - lock a dedicated object instance, never `this`, a `Type` or an interned string, because callers may take those same locks - and from C# 13 / .NET 9 the dedicated type is `System.Threading.Lock`, whose `EnterScope()` returns a `ref struct` that the `using`/`lock` statement disposes, so the release happens even on exceptions. Two further language facts shape the pattern: `await` is not allowed inside a lock body (the guardian is thread-affine, so asynchronous work must be queued or guarded by a `SemaphoreSlim`), and locks must be acquired in a consistent order across nested guardians - the API reference warns that the inverse order deadlocks. What replaces the classic structure is therefore not a different lock but the *choice* of lock object: a private instance per invariant instead of a public one, with `Monitor` as the underlying non-C# 13 implementation.
pitfalls: Locking `this`, a `Type` or a string literal (or any object a caller can reach) lets outside code hold the guardian's lock; the gate must be private and used for nothing else.

`await` inside a `lock` body is a compile error and a `System.Threading.Tasks` continuation may resume on another thread, so asynchronous work under the guard needs `SemaphoreSlim` or a queue instead.

The gate must be `readonly` and per-instance: reassigning it, or sharing one static gate across state that could have its own, either drops the protection or widens contention and reorders lock acquisition into deadlock.

variants.name: Dedicated System.Threading.Lock with EnterScope
variants.implementation_notes: From C# 13 / .NET 9 the gate should be a `System.Threading.Lock` instead of a bare `object`: the compiler recognises the type and lowers `lock (_gate)` to `using (_gate.EnterScope())`, a dedicated non-recursive mutual-exclusion type with a scope-based release, and warns when a known `Lock` is cast to something else and locked in a way that would silently fall back to `Monitor`. Use it whenever the target framework allows - it is the platform's own 'guardian' type and the closest C# comes to owning the guarded state. The `object`-gate form remains correct and portable for older targets, and `Monitor.Wait`/`Pulse` (unavailable on `Lock`) is still the reason to keep a plain object gate when the guardian must also implement guarded waiting.
pitfalls: The `lock` statement only lowers to `Lock.EnterScope()` when the expression's static type is exactly `System.Threading.Lock`; a cast or an interface-typed variable falls back to `Monitor` on the same object without a warning in that path.
`System.Threading.Lock` has no `Wait`/`Pulse`: a guardian that needs condition waiting must keep `Monitor` (object gate) or use `SemaphoreSlim`/`Channel` beside it.
